title: Gukesh holds Sindarov to a draw in Game 1 after recovering from a big time deficit
dek: The champion defended a Berlin Endgame with Black in Cologny and takes White in Game 2 tonight at 7.30 pm IST.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
D. Gukesh began the defence of his world chess title with a draw against Javokhir Sindarov on Tuesday, holding the Uzbek challenger in Game 1 in Cologny, near Geneva, after falling well behind on the clock. Gukesh takes the white pieces for the first time in the match in Game 2 on Wednesday, starting at 7.30 pm IST.

The game ended in a draw by threefold repetition after 38 moves, leaving the score at 0.5-0.5 in the 14-game match. The first player to 7.5 points becomes world champion.

## How the game went

Sindarov, with White, steered the game into the Berlin Endgame, one of the most solid lines in top-level chess, and then surprised Gukesh with a new move, 13.Ne4. Gukesh spent more than 15 minutes on his reply and fell about 25 minutes behind on the clock, according to reports.

When Sindarov played 21.g4, which was not the computer engines' first choice, he led by about half an hour, and Gukesh had 16 minutes left for his next 20 moves, with no time added per move until the first time control at move 40. Sindarov then gave up a pawn temporarily to keep up the pressure, but Gukesh defended precisely, playing quickly once the game reached positions he had prepared, and the danger passed.

There was a brief moment of confusion at the end: Sindarov first claimed the draw incorrectly and was penalised two minutes on his clock before the repetition was confirmed. Under the match rules, players cannot simply agree a draw before Black's 40th move; before then a game can only be drawn by repetition or stalemate, claimed through the arbiter.

## What the players said

At the press conference, Gukesh said he had felt in control throughout and did not "really need to be worried", according to reports. Sindarov said his opponent had "defended very well".

## The match so far

For Gukesh, a solid start with Black is a useful result. He came into the match as the lower-rated player: on November's rating list Sindarov is world number four at 2782, while Gukesh is 26th at 2710, and Sindarov leads their classical head-to-head record. Gukesh, 20, became the youngest undisputed world champion when he beat China's Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024. Sindarov, also 20, earned his challenge by winning this year's Candidates Tournament in Cyprus without losing a game.

Sindarov has White in the odd-numbered games and Gukesh in the even-numbered ones. Game 3 is on Thursday, followed by the first rest day on 27 November. The match is scheduled to end with Game 14 on 11 December, with tiebreaks, if needed, on 12 December. Each player has 120 minutes for the first 40 moves and then 30 more minutes, with 30 seconds added per move from move 41. If the match is tied 7-7, it goes to rapid games, then faster rapid games and blitz until there is a winner. The prize fund is $2.5 million, and each player earns $200,000 for every game he wins.
